```text
   This is a fantastic question and one we should all be concerned with! Re-
cent research shows that the brain starts shrinking around the age of 30
and shrinks on the order of 5% every decade thereafter, unless you take
steps to prevent it. Data is starting to be produced that show you can stop
this process and, if you work at it, you can actually grow your brain!
   Most people think that memory decline is a normal part of aging, but it
doesn’t have to be. There are five factors that have been shown to be
particularly good for your brain as you age:

   ♠ Engage in learning activities. Luckily, you play poker and it is a
       fantastic mechanism for keeping the brain sharp. Your brain works
       off of the “use it or lose it” maxim, so it is very important to keep
       on learning. The less you use your brain to learn more things, the
       less able it is to learn. Learning helps build neural connections and
       the more connections you have, the less likely it is you will
       experience cognitive decline. Try to make your learning active –
       take notes, analyze situations, attempt to memorize things, and
       critically evaluate information. Keep challenging yourself
       intellectually, and your brain will thank you.
   ♠ Diet is crucial to a healthy brain. As discussed in Chapter 9, there
       are certain foods that help your brain and some that hurt it. A
       good diet provides the foundation of neurotransmitters and helps
       your brain create brain-derived neurotrophic factor (which has
       been called Miracle-Gro for the brain because you need it for
       neuron growth). Not surprisingly, a diet filled with processed foods
       that is high in sugar, sodium, and trans-fats is bad for the brain.
       Diabetes, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol are leading
       known brain shrinkers and can be avoided in most cases by making
       dietary changes.
   ♠ Regular exercise keeps the brain sharp. We know that regular
       exercise improves brain chemistry and makes it function better.
```

```text
Q2) Left and Right Brain
      Is one side of the brain used more than the other in poker? If
      so does that give an edge to a player [who] uses that side of
      the brain more?
                                                                       Dave

    Most people have heard that creative, imaginative, and artistic people
are right-brain dominant, and that left-brain dominant people are analyti-
cal, logical, and well organized. This would lead you to believe that being
left-brain dominant might confer benefits at the poker table.
    It turns out that the left-brain–right-brain dichotomy is a myth. Re-
cently scientists at the University of Utah conducted a two-year study of
brain function (Nielsen et al., 2013). Over the two-year period, they
studied the brain functions of 1,011 participants who ranged in age from
7 to 29. The scientists conducted brain scans using functional MRI analy-
sis. They looked at activity in 7,000 brain regions and analyzed neural
connections within and between these regions. While the researchers saw
some areas of heavy neural traffic in particular regions of the brain, on
balance, both sides of the brain were equal in neural networks and con-
nectivity. In other words, they did not find left-brain or right-brain domi-
nance in any of the study participants.
```

```text
                                                         Readers’ Questions

Q3) Banishing Fear
      Yoda says that fear is the path to the dark side, and I think he’s
      right. If I play the first day of a multi-day MTT really well and
      bag a decent chip stack (50BB), going into Day 2 I often find
      myself feeling afraid to lose. How do you banish the fear and
      carry the confidence of strong play from Day 1 into Day 2?
                                                                           Nancy

   I’m excited to tackle this question because it is one that a lot of players
can probably relate to! No one likes to lose money, but it is an inescapable
part of poker. There is no method of playing that can guarantee that you
will never lose, and taking rational risks to finish in the top three spots is
the correct play in MTTs.
   Psychological research shows that losing affects us to such a great de-
gree that it shows up on imaging scans of the brain as pain. Daniel Kah-
neman and Amos Tversky have studied and described loss aversion in
great detail. They found that loss aversion is a quirk in the mental machin-
ery. It is hardwired into us to avoid losses, and that aversion is strongest
when we are asked to make choices that involve risk. According to them,
evolution has made us abhor losses, and we can get particularly sticky
about losing something we have in hand (like our chips). Across numerous
studies, psychologists have quantified that the impact of a loss is 2–2.5
times greater than the impact of a gain of the same size. Thus, losses
loom larger in our minds. We will remember losses more vividly than wins
and feel them more intensely.
   There is another side to the findings of Kahneman and Tversky. They
also found that people tend to get more conservative when holding gains
and seek to “protect” what they have acquired. So it is likely that when
you are going into Day 2, your mind is fixating on not losing your chips
you worked so hard to acquire on Day 1. You want to hold onto your gain
and may even be willing to settle for a sure thing min-cash instead of
risking your stack to go for the eventual win.
```

```text
Peak Poker Performance

   Coping with fear and anxiety is a significant challenge for many poker
players. The trick is to understand that you can feel fear and not let it dis-
rupt your judgments or decisions. You have to realize that your mind is cre-
ating this fear, but you are not forced to react to it. You can notice it and
accept that fear is a normal reaction to anything outside of your comfort
zone. Most of us have a bad relationship with fear. We try to run from it
instead of realizing that we get scared when we bump up against the edge
of our comfort zones. Our infinite potential lies on the other side of our
comfort zone and we have to break through if we want to realize it.
   It is very difficult to banish fear as it is nearly impossible to push any
emotion out of our awareness using typical control mechanisms. A quick
way to de-activate the amygdala is to use a “noting practice.” You take
note of your feelings by saying to yourself, “I notice that I am feeling fear
right now.” The best way to overcome negative feelings is to notice them,
accept them, and move on to making the most +EV decisions you can.
   Just remember, loss aversion is a significant psychological hurdle that
must be overcome in order to be a successful poker player. Loss aversion
promotes irrational behavior – like playing too tight when it is not war-
ranted. Anytime your behavior becomes too rigid, the likely result is more
losses and not less.
   I asked Jonathan to give his thoughts on this question and here’s what
he said:

      You have to recognize that making Day 2 is not too impor-
      tant, especially if you are playing in a manner that maximizes
      your chances of winning. All you can do in poker is make the
      best possible play each time you have a decision. When you
      buy in, you have to treat that money as if it is gone. Your goal
      should not be to “get that money back” by min-cashing. You
      must constantly play with the intention of maximizing your
      equity. That often means attempting plays that put your en-
      tire stack at risk. Sometimes that is what it takes to be as
      profitable as possible.


238
```

```text
                                                          Readers’ Questions

Q4) Moving Up
      My question is how do I learn to deal with the mental aspects
      of the climbing up in stakes? How do I learn to deal with the
      stress of playing bigger pots?
                                                                          Wout

    I feel like this question has some similarities to Nancy’s in that fear is at
least partially part of the problem. There are several things that come to
mind that might help you. First, you need to make sure that you are prop-
erly rolled for the games you are playing. It is hard to disassociate from
the money if you are playing outside of your roll. Disassociating from
money is a skill that can be learned. We had Paul Otto on a recent episode
of the The Mindset Advantage podcast , and he gave a tip for learning to
disconnect from the money. He suggested converting everything to big
blinds (BBs). Thinking about pots as BBs instead of cold, hard cash can
make it less stressful.
    Second, you need to build up your confidence by improving your skill
set. You are not likely to play at your best if you feel like you are out-
classed by your opponents. You have to be honest about where you are at
in your skill development. A large part of being a successful poker player is
game selection. You want to select games where you will have a good
shot at making a profit.
```
